annotations.annotation_text: Page 48 opens Book 1, Chapter 3 ("The Trial of HCE") during the Age of Gods phase. This passage continues the public trial and persecution of HCE, the ballad of Hosty, and the testimony of witnesses, featuring HCE, the Twelve Jurors, Hosty. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.

annotations.annotation_text: Chapter 3 is deeply modeled on judicial proceedings, complete with witnesses, testimony, and cross-examination. HCE's guilt is interrogated publicly.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp

annotations.annotation_text: The Four Old Men (Mamalujo) act as judges here. They represent the Four Evangelists and the Four Provinces of Ireland (Ulster, Munster, Leinster, Connacht).
sources: McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/annotationstofin0000mchu_h5g8

annotations.annotation_text: HCE is tried in absentia. He is the sleeping dreamer, incapacitated and unable to speak in his own defense against the growing rumors.
sources: Gordon, John. Finnegans Wake: A Plot Summary. https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com

annotations.annotation_text: Issy/daughter figure "maggies" on page 48 ("The Trial of HCE"): the narcissistic mirror-daughter, modeled on Isolde and Swift's dual muses Stella and Vanessa, appears here within the public trial and persecution of HCE, the ballad of Hosty, and the testimony of witnesses. Her prismatic splitting into twenty-eight Rainbow Girls reflects the cycle's Age of Gods phase through youthful seduction and self-reflection.
sources: Bédier, Joseph. The Romance of Tristan and Iseult. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/14244
Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 48 ("The Trial of HCE"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Gods dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind

annotations.annotation_text: The twelve jurors condemning HCE correlate with the twelve apostles, the twelve months of the year, and the signs of the zodiac.
sources: Glasheen, Adaline. Third Census of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/thirdcensusoffin0000glas

annotations.annotation_text: The testimony of various witnesses in the trial, often unreliable and conflicting, adding to the kaleidoscopic nature of truth in the Wake.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
